title: UniTo: where it stands and where it could go
text:
Provisional results. The corpora are being validated: every number may change.
The University of Turin (UniTo) has about 300 publications on sustainable plastics. The Sustainability profile and Indicators pages show what it does today. This page looks ahead, with one idea: an organisation grows most easily into areas, and with partners, that are close to what it already does (proximity).

title: UniTo: where it stands and where it could go
section: Research areas close to UniTo’s strengths
text:
Research areas close to UniTo’s strengths
Each circle is a research area (an OpenAlex subfield) in which UniTo is not yet specialised. To the right, the area is closer to UniTo’s current strengths: it is related to many areas where UniTo is already specialised (two areas are related when the same institutions around the world tend to be specialised in both). Higher up, the area grows faster than research on sustainable plastics as a whole (its share of the publications in 2020–2025 compared with 2010–2019; above the dashed line, it is growing). The areas that are both close and growing are the natural candidates: to strengthen where UniTo already has some publications, to enter where it has few.

opp = FileAttachment("data/unito_opportunities.csv").csv({typed: true})
notSpecialised = opp.filter(d => d.quadrant !== "UniTo specialised")
quadrants = ["close and growing", "close, not growing", "distant, growing", "distant, not growing"]























Plot.plot({
  width, height: 520,
  x: {label: "Closeness to UniTo's strengths (density) →", grid: true},
  y: {label: "↑ Growth (share 2020–25 / share 2010–19)", grid: true},
  color: {domain: quadrants, range: ["#c8102e", "#eda100", "#2a78d6", "#b4b2a9"], legend: true},
  r: {range: [2, 14]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([1], {stroke: "#888", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.dot(notSpecialised, {x: "density", y: "growth", r: "works", fill: "quadrant", fillOpacity: 0.75,
      stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 0.5,
      title: d => `${d.subfield} (${d.field})\nUniTo: ${d.unito_papers} publications\ngrowth ×${d.growth}\nmain category: ${d.main_category}${d.action ? "\nsuggestion: " + d.action : ""}`,
      tip: true})
  ]
})







Circle size: the publications of the area in the whole corpus. Hover on a circle for details. The table lists the areas that are close and growing.


Inputs.table(opp.filter(d => d.quadrant === "close and growing").sort((a, b) => b.density - a.density), {
  columns: ["subfield", "action", "unito_papers", "unito_rca", "density", "growth"],
  header: {subfield: "Research area", field: "Field", action: "Suggestion", unito_papers: "UniTo publications",
           unito_rca: "UniTo index", density: "Closeness", growth: "Growth", main_category: "Main category"},
  rows: 26
})

title: UniTo: where it stands and where it could go
section: UniTo’s partners in Piedmont, Italy and Europe
text:
UniTo’s partners in Piedmont, Italy and Europe
Every institution in Europe that has published on sustainable plastics with UniTo, and the new candidates: institutions that have never published with UniTo but are likely to, given their proximity to UniTo (in topics, in space, and through common partners). The likelihood comes from a model trained on how new collaborations between European universities started in 2020–2025.







Circle size: joint publications with UniTo. Click on a circle for details. Partners outside Europe are not shown.

The position paper of the project (section 6, Strategies for UniTo) discusses these results, together with the companies that use UniTo’s research.

title: Maps
text:
Provisional results. The corpora are being validated: every number may change.

The maps open in VOSviewer Online, the web version of VOSviewer, a tool widely used to draw maps of science. In a map, each circle is a topic, a technology, a country or an organisation; its size is the number of documents; a line joins two circles that appear together in the same documents. Circles close to each other are strongly linked, and circles of the same colour form a group (a cluster). Zoom with the mouse wheel, drag to move, and click on a circle to see its details.

title: Research and innovation on sustainable plastics
text:
Provisional results. The two collections of documents behind these pages (publications and patents) are still being validated. Every number may change.
Plastics are central to the ecological transition: they are made, used and thrown away on a huge scale, and they are one of the main sources of pollution. “Sustainable plastics” covers many different efforts: plastics made from renewable sources, plastics that biodegrade, recycling, cleaner chemistry, the study of microplastics and of the risks to health.
BRIDgeS (Bridging Research and Innovation Dynamics for Sustainable plastics) is a project of the University of Turin (UniTo) that maps who does research and who invents in this field, worldwide, and where UniTo stands. It uses about 315,000 scientific publications (from OpenAlex, 1980–2025) and about 314,000 patent families (from PATSTAT, 1980–2025), each read against a set of keywords built with experts and sorted into eight categories, C1–C8.

A document can belong to several categories. The Data and method page explains how the documents were collected and how to read the numbers.

title: Data and method
text: Provisional results. A sample of the documents is being checked by hand and with a language model, to measure how many of the documents found are really about sustainable plastics. The collections will then be cleaned, and every number on this website will be updated.

title: Data and method
text:
How the documents were found

Keywords. The project team, with a survey of experts, built two lists of keywords: one for scientific publications and one for patents. Each keyword belongs to one of eight categories, C1–C8 (see the home page).
Publications. The keywords were searched in the titles and abstracts of OpenAlex, an open catalogue of the world’s scientific publications. About 315,000 publications from 1980 to 2025.
Patents. The same approach on the titles and abstracts of PATSTAT (European Patent Office), together with the technology classes of patents that are specific to sustainable plastics. Patents are counted as families: all the patents that protect the same invention in different countries count once. About 314,000 families from 1980 to 2025, by the year of the first filing.
Categories. A document is in a category when it matches at least one of the category’s keywords. A document can be in several categories.

title: Data and method
text:
How to read the numbers

Who is an actor. For publications, the institutions and countries in the authors’ affiliations. For patents, the applicants (the owners) and, for countries and regions, the address of the inventors.
Full counts. A document written by two countries counts once for each.
The University of Turin is the OpenAlex record of the university together with the institutions that OpenAlex places under it. The university hospital (AOU Città della Salute e della Scienza, San Luigi Gonzaga) and Politecnico di Torino are separate actors.
Names in patents are written as in the patent documents and are not yet harmonised: the same company can appear under two spellings.
Addresses. Many patents have no address for applicants or inventors, so regional numbers (Piedmont) are underestimated.

The project

title: Indicators
section: How to keep the indicators up to date
text:
How to keep the indicators up to date
The indicators are computed by scripts, so they can be renewed every year: the two collections of documents are downloaded again with the same keywords (OpenAlex for publications, PATSTAT for patents), the analysis scripts are run again, and this website is rebuilt. Comparing one year’s numbers with the previous year’s shows whether an actor is growing, changing its profile, or building new links.

title: Sustainability profile
text:
Provisional results. The corpora are being validated: every number may change.

Choose the documents (publications or patents), an actor and an actor to compare it with. The first chart shows the share of the actor’s documents in each of the eight categories; the second its specialisation index, its share divided by the world’s share (above 1: the actor works on that category more than the world average); the third how its profile changed over time.

actors  = FileAttachment("data/profile_actors.csv").csv({typed: true})
cats    = FileAttachment("data/categories.csv").csv()
// periods and trend are read as text and the counts made numbers by hand:
// the automatic reading would take labels such as "2015-19" for dates
toNumbers = rows => rows.map(d => {
  const o = {...d}
  for (const k of ["n", ...cats.map(c => c.category)]) o[k] = +d[k]
  return o
})
periods = toNumbers(await FileAttachment("data/profile_periods.csv").csv())
trend   = toNumbers(await FileAttachment("data/profile_trend.csv").csv())

// R writes TRUE/FALSE: read them as yes/no
isTrue = v => v === true || v === "TRUE"
// the colours of the eight categories (the same as the graphs of the paper)
catColours = ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4", "#008300", "#6250d6", "#e34948"]
fmt = n => n.toLocaleString("en")
pct = x => (100 * x).toFixed(1) + "%"



































































viewof corpus = Inputs.radio(["Publications", "Patents"], {label: "Documents", value: "Publications"})
viewof actorType = Inputs.select(["Research organisation", "Company", "Country", "Area"],
                                 {label: "Type of actor", value: "Research organisation"})
viewof piedmontOnly = Inputs.toggle({label: "Only Piedmont", value: false})























choices = actors
  .filter(d => d.corpus === corpus && d.actor_type === actorType && (!piedmontOnly || isTrue(d.piedmont)))
  .sort((a, b) => b.docs - a.docs)

// UniTo is chosen at the start, when it is in the list
viewof actor = Inputs.select(choices, {
  label: "Actor",
  format: d => `${d.actor} (${fmt(d.docs)})`,
  value: choices.find(d => d.actor === "UniTo" || d.actor === "UNIVERSITA DEGLI STUDI DI TORINO")
})
















others = actors.filter(d => d.corpus === corpus)
  .sort((a, b) => (a.actor_type === "Area" ? 0 : 1) - (b.actor_type === "Area" ? 0 : 1) || b.docs - a.docs)
viewof other = Inputs.select(others, {
  label: "Compare with",
  format: d => `${d.actor} (${fmt(d.docs)})`,
  value: others.find(d => d.actor_id === "A:World")
})
viewof period = Inputs.radio(["All years", "1980-1999", "2000-2014", "2015-2025"],
                             {label: "Period", value: "All years"})























Numbers in brackets: documents in 1980–2025. Patents: countries and regions by the inventors’ address; organisations by the applicants.



rowOf = a => a ? periods.find(d => d.corpus === corpus && d.actor_id === a.actor_id && d.period === period) : undefined
profileOf = a => {
  const r = rowOf(a)
  if (!r || r.n === 0) return []
  return cats.map(c => ({who: a.actor, category: c.name, k: r[c.category], n: r.n, share: r[c.category] / r.n}))
}
p1 = profileOf(actor)
p2 = (other && actor && other.actor_id !== actor.actor_id) ? profileOf(other) : []
world = profileOf(actors.find(d => d.corpus === corpus && d.actor_id === "A:World"))





































// a sentence that sums up the profile
{
  if (!actor) return md`*No actor of this type here: choose another type, or switch off "Only Piedmont".*`
  if (p1.length === 0) return md`**${actor.actor}** has no ${corpus.toLowerCase()} in ${period}.`
  const top = [...p1].sort((a, b) => b.share - a.share)[0]
  const spec = p1.map((d, i) => ({...d, index: d.share / world[i].share}))
                 .filter(d => d.k >= 5).sort((a, b) => b.index - a.index)[0]
  return md`**${actor.actor}** · ${fmt(p1[0].n)} ${corpus.toLowerCase()} (${period}).
  Its largest category is **${top.category}** (${pct(top.share)} of its documents)${spec ?
  `; the one where it is most specialised is **${spec.category}** (${spec.index.toFixed(2)} times the world's share).` : "."}`
}







// 1. The share of the documents in each category: the actor and the comparison
Plot.plot({
  width, height: 460, marginLeft: 200,
  x: {label: "Share of the documents (%) →", percent: true, grid: true},
  y: {axis: null},
  fy: {label: null, domain: cats.map(c => c.name)},
  color: {domain: [actor?.actor, other?.actor], range: ["#c8102e", "#9a9a9a"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX([...p1, ...p2], {x: "share", y: "who", fy: "category", fill: "who",
      title: d => `${d.who}\n${d.category}\n${fmt(d.k)} of ${fmt(d.n)} documents (${pct(d.share)})`, tip: true}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})







A document can be in several categories, so the shares do not add up to 100%.


Specialisation compared with the world

spec = p1.map((d, i) => ({...d, index: d.share / world[i].share, few: d.k < 5})).filter(d => d.k > 0)
actor?.actor_id === "A:World" ? md`*The world is the reference: its index is 1 in every category.*` :
Plot.plot({
  width, height: 300, marginLeft: 200,
  x: {type: "log", label: "Specialisation index (1 = world average, log scale) →", grid: true, tickFormat: "~g"},
  y: {label: null, domain: cats.map(c => c.name)},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(spec, {y: "category", x1: d => 1, x2: "index",
      fill: d => d.index >= 1 ? "#c8102e" : "#9a9a9a", fillOpacity: d => d.few ? 0.35 : 1,
      title: d => `${d.category}\nindex ${d.index.toFixed(2)} · ${fmt(d.k)} documents${d.few ? " (few)" : ""}`, tip: true}),
    Plot.ruleX([1], {strokeWidth: 1.5})
  ]
})

















Over time

trendRows = actor ? trend.filter(d => d.corpus === corpus && d.actor_id === actor.actor_id) : []
trendLong = trendRows.filter(d => d.n >= 10)
  .flatMap(d => cats.map(c => ({window: d.period, category: c.name, k: d[c.category], n: d.n, share: d[c.category] / d.n})))
windows = ["1980-84", "1985-89", "1990-94", "1995-99", "2000-04", "2005-09", "2010-14", "2015-19", "2020-25"]

Plot.plot({
  width, height: 150, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {domain: windows, label: null},
  y: {label: "Documents", grid: true},
  marks: [Plot.barY(trendRows, {x: "period", y: "n", fill: "#54565a", title: d => `${d.period}: ${fmt(d.n)} documents`, tip: true}),
          Plot.ruleY([0])]
})






























trendLong.length === 0 ? md`*Too few documents to show a trend.*` :
Plot.plot({
  width, height: 360, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {domain: windows, label: "Five-year window"},
  y: {label: "Share of the documents (%)", percent: true, grid: true},
  color: {domain: cats.map(c => c.name), range: catColours, legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(trendLong, {x: "window", y: "share", stroke: "category", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.dot(trendLong, {x: "window", y: "share", fill: "category", r: 3,
      title: d => `${d.category}\n${d.window}: ${fmt(d.k)} of ${fmt(d.n)} (${pct(d.share)})`, tip: true})
  ]
})







The last window, 2020–25, has six years.
